title: Acentos regionales
subtitle: Buenos Aires, the Caribbean, Mexico, Bogotá, the Andes

lessons.title: Rioplatense: ll and y as "sh"
lessons.goal: Recognise the Buenos Aires and Montevideo pronunciation of ll and y, and keep it apart from ch.

tip.title: "Sho me shamo"
tip.body: Around the Río de la Plata (Buenos Aires, Montevideo), ll and consonant y are not the soft [ʝ] of Madrid or Mexico City but a hissing sound: [ʒ], like the s in English "measure", or, especially among younger speakers in Buenos Aires, [ʃ], like English "sh". So "yo me llamo" sounds like "sho me shamo", "calle" like "cashe", "playa" like "plasha". To do it, round your lips slightly and push air through the middle of your tongue, exactly as for "sh", with or without voice. Careful: ch stays different. Ch starts with a tiny t: "cacho" is ca-tcho, while Rioplatense "cayo" is ca-sho. The vowel y (y, hoy, muy) never changes. Other things you'll hear in the same region: voseo (vos sos, vos tenés, with the stress on the last syllable), a melody that many people compare to Italian, and s that is often softened to an h before a consonant ("mismo" ≈ "mihmo"). The narrator here uses Madrid pronunciation; listen to the story to hear the Buenos Aires voices.

phrases.note: Buenos Aires: "sho me shamo"; Madrid and most of Latin America: a soft y-sound.
Argentina, Uruguay: vos sos = tú eres.

phrases.t: La calle está llena de gente.
phrases.n: The street is full of people.

phrases.note: colectivo = bus in Argentina. Buenos Aires: sha she-gó.

stress.note: Voseo forms stress the last syllable: sos, tenés, querés.

story.title: Una llamada a Buenos Aires
story.intro: Pablo from Madrid calls two friends in Buenos Aires: listen to how differently they say ll and y.

lines.name: Pablo
lines.t: ¡Hola! Yo me llamo Pablo y soy de Madrid.
lines.n: Hi! My name is Pablo and I'm from Madrid.

lines.name: Elena
lines.t: ¡Hola, Pablo! Yo me llamo Elena y soy de Buenos Aires.
lines.n: Hi, Pablo! My name is Elena and I'm from Buenos Aires.

lines.name: Pablo
lines.t: ¿Qué tiempo hace allí? Aquí llueve sin parar.
lines.n: What's the weather like there? Here it rains non-stop.

lines.name: Elena
lines.t: Acá hace calor. Ayer fuimos al parque con mi hermano y llevamos el mate.
lines.n: It's hot here. Yesterday my brother and I went to the park and took the mate.

lines.name: Tomás
lines.t: ¡Hola, Pablo! Yo soy el hermano. ¿Vos ya conocés Buenos Aires?
lines.n: Hi, Pablo! I'm the brother. Have you been to Buenos Aires yet?

lines.name: Pablo
lines.t: Todavía no, pero ya tengo el billete para mayo.
lines.n: Not yet, but I've already got my ticket for May.

lines.name: Tomás
lines.t: ¡Qué bueno! Traé un paraguas, por las dudas.
lines.n: Great! Bring an umbrella, just in case.

lines.name: Elena
lines.n: And call us when you arrive!

questions.n: What did they take to the park?
When is Pablo going to travel?

prompts.n: Ask someone where they're from, using vos.

lessons.title: Lost s, Mexican melody, Bogotá clarity
lessons.goal: Understand aspirated s and recognise Mexican, Colombian and Andean features.

tip.title: Same language, different music
tip.body: Aspirated s: in the Caribbean (Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic, coastal Venezuela and Colombia), in Andalusia and the Canary Islands, and around the Río de la Plata, s at the end of a syllable is often softened to an h-like breath or dropped: "los amigos" ≈ "loh amigo", "mismo" ≈ "mihmo", "¿cómo estás?" ≈ "¿cómo ehtá?". Plurals and "tú" forms then depend on context; in eastern Andalusia the vowel before the lost s is often pronounced more open, which keeps some of the difference. Pronounce every s yourself; just be ready to hear it disappear. Mexico (especially the centre): consonants are kept firm and s is strong, while unstressed vowels next to s are often shortened or nearly whispered ("pues" ≈ "ps", "entonces" ≈ "ntons's"); the melody often rises and stretches the last stressed syllable. Bogotá: speech is often described as clear and careful, every consonant pronounced, and usted is used a lot, even among friends and family. Andean Spanish (highlands of Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador): s is usually strong, unstressed vowels may weaken, and in some areas ll and y are still two different sounds.

phrases.note: Polite Mexican reply when you didn't hear or are called.

phrases.n: Can I have a black coffee, please? (Colombia)
phrases.note: "Regalar" is a polite way to ask for something in Colombia; tinto = black coffee.

stress.note: Say every s; aspirating accents soften all three.

stress.n: Can I have a black coffee, please?

stress.note: Six s sounds: in Havana or Seville many of them may become a soft h.

story.title: Tres acentos en un congreso
story.intro: At a conference, a Mexican, a Colombian and a Spaniard meet and help each other find a room.

lines.name: Jorge
lines.t: Buenas tardes. Soy Jorge y vengo de Guadalajara.
lines.n: Good afternoon. I'm Jorge and I come from Guadalajara.

lines.name: Salomé
lines.t: Mucho gusto, Jorge. Yo soy Salomé, de Bogotá. ¿Usted es profesor?
lines.n: Nice to meet you, Jorge. I'm Salomé, from Bogotá. Are you a teacher?

lines.name: Jorge
lines.t: Sí, doy clases de historia. ¿Y usted?
lines.n: Yes, I teach history. And you?

lines.name: Salomé
lines.t: Yo trabajo en una editorial. Me encanta escuchar tantos acentos distintos.
lines.n: I work at a publishing house. I love hearing so many different accents.

lines.name: Carmen
lines.t: Hola, soy Carmen, de Valladolid. Perdón, ¿es aquí la sala de prensa?
lines.n: Hi, I'm Carmen, from Valladolid. Sorry, is this the press room?

lines.name: Jorge
lines.n: Yes, it's here. Come in, come in!

lines.name: Salomé
lines.t: Siga, siga, que ya va a empezar.
lines.n: Come in, it's about to start.

lines.name: Carmen
lines.t: Gracias. Tres acentos distintos y nos entendemos perfectamente.
lines.n: Thanks. Three different accents and we understand each other perfectly.

prompts.n: Ask for a black coffee the Colombian way.
t: Me regala un tinto por favor
